text: Jose Maria Canlas Sison (Tagalog: [hoˈse mɐˈɾija kɐnˈlas ˈsisɔn]; February 8, 1939 – December 16, 2022), also known as Joma, was a Filipino writer, poet, and activist who founded and led the Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP) and developed a philosophy based on Marxism–Leninism-Maoism, known as National Democracy. Born in Cabugao, Ilocos Sur, to a prominent landowning family with Spanish-Mexican-Malay mestizo and Fujian, Chinese ancestry, and connections to clans such as the Crisólogos, Geraldinos, Vergaras, Azcuetas, Sollers, Serranos, and Singsons, Sison was the son of Salustiano Sison, a strong supporter of Claro Mayo Recto with a mix of feudalist and anti-imperialist views, and Florentina Canlas Sison, from a landed family in Mexico, Pampanga. As a child, he was nicknamed "Cheng" by his parents. His great-grandfather, Don Leandro Serrano, was the largest landlord in northern Luzon at the end of the 19th century; his grandfather, Don Gorgonio Soller Sison, was the last gobernadorcillo of Cabugao under Spanish rule, the municipal president during the Philippine revolutionary government, and the first mayor under U.S. colonial rule; his great-uncle, Don Marcelino Crisólogo, was the first governor of Ilocos Sur; his uncle, Teófilo Sison, served as governor of Pangasinan and the first Defense Secretary in the Commonwealth government, though he was convicted in 1946 for collaborating with Japanese occupation forces and later amnestied in 1947. During his childhood in Ilocos, he learned about the Huk rebellion from Ilocano farm workers and his mother, and in Manila, he discussed Hukbalahap activities with his barber. He attended public school before entering Ateneo de Manila University and later Colegio de San Juan de Letran, graduating from the University of the Philippines in 1959 with a Bachelor of Arts in English literature with honors, and then studied Indonesian in Indonesia before returning to the Philippines to become a professor of literature, Rizal studies, and political science. He joined the Partido Komunista ng Pilipinas (PKP) in December 1962 and became a member of its executive committee in early 1963; he also served as Vice Chairman of the Lapiang Manggagawa (which later became the Socialist Party) and general secretary of the Movement for the Advancement of Nationalism. In 1964, he co-founded the Kabataang Makabayan ("Patriotic Youth") with Nilo S. Tayag, which organized youth against the Vietnam War, Ferdinand Marcos, imperialism, bureaucrat capitalism, and feudalism, and promoted the study of Maoism. On December 26, 1968, he formed and led the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP), which was founded on Marxism–Leninism-Maoism and established a two-stage revolution: national-democratic as the first stage, followed by socialist revolution. This period, known as the First Great Rectification Movement, involved Sison and other radical youth criticizing the existing PKP leadership, which had been dominated by Moscow-leaning general secretaries from the Lava family. During this time, Sison used the nom de guerre Amado Guerrero ("beloved warrior") and published the manifesto Philippine Society and Revolution. After the reorganization, the CPP gained a larger base and a renewed political line. On March 29, 1969, the CPP, along with an Huk faction led by Bernabe Buscayno, organized the New People's Army (NPA), a guerrilla-military wing with over 110 fronts nationwide covering 75 of the 81 Philippine provinces, which aims to wage a peasant-worker revolutionary war against landlords and foreign companies through rural and mountain operations. Sison was arrested on November 8, 1977, in La Union during the Marcos presidency and imprisoned for nearly nine years, mostly in solitary confinement, during which he wrote prolifically, including Basic Principles of Marxism-Leninism: A Primer, which his wife Julie de Lima smuggled out in 1982. He was released on March 5, 1986, after the People Power Revolution, by President Corazon Aquino for "national reconciliation" and for his opposition to Marcos, though his release was protested by the military. He published Prison & Beyond, a poetry book that won the Southeast Asia WRITE award. After returning to teach at the University of the Philippines, he began a global lecture tour in September 1986, during which he actively sought to discredit the Aquino administration in European media, citing human rights violations such as the Mendiola massacre. In October 1986, he received the Southeast Asia Writers Award from the Crown Prince of Thailand in Bangkok. In 1989, he was cited in Gregg Jones' book Red Revolution as having coordinated the Plaza Miranda bombing in August 1971. Since 1987, Sison based himself in the Netherlands for his lecture tours. In September 1988, his passport was revoked and he was charged under the Philippines' Anti-Subversion Act; he applied for political asylum in the Netherlands, which was denied, but Dutch and European law protected him from deportation. Since 1992, he lived in the Netherlands as a recognized political refugee. The CPP stated for over 20 years that Sison was no longer involved in operational decisions and served as chief political consultant of the National Democratic Front (NDF) in peace negotiations. On August 28, 2007, the Dutch National Criminal Investigation Department arrested Sison in Utrecht for alleged involvement in three assassinations in the Philippines: the 2003 murder of Romulo Kintanar and the 2006 murders of Arturo Tabara and Stephen Ong. His apartment and those of co-workers were searched. Around 100 left-wing activists held a demonstration in Manila on August 30, 2007, which was quickly ended by police. There were no plans to extradite him to the Philippines, as no extradition request was filed and the crimes occurred in the Netherlands. Dutch lawyer Victor Koppe stated Sison would plead not guilty and could face life imprisonment. On September 1, 2007, the Dutch court confirmed that Sison was being maltreated, held in solitary confinement without access to media, visitors, or prescription medicines, and accused the Dutch government of being aligned with the Philippine government of Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo and the U.S. The CPP feared Sison might be subjected to "extra-judicial" transfer to the United States, possibly to Guantanamo Bay or a secret facility. U.S. Ambassador Kristie Ann Kenney announced U.S. support for the Dutch prosecution. In New York, former U.S. Attorney General Ramsey Clark called for Sison's release and joined his legal defense team led by Belgian lawyer Jan Fermon, questioning the validity of the charges, which had already been dismissed by the Philippine Supreme Court. Committee DEFEND claimed the Dutch government tortured Sison at the National Penitentiary in Scheveningen, and his wife Julie De Lima was denied access to him for medicine and warm clothing. Sison's counsel, Romeo Capulong, challenged Dutch jurisdiction, noting the Philippine Supreme Court had dismissed the cases on July 2. On September 7, 2007, the Dutch court heard defense arguments and stated it would issue a ruling on extending detention. Supporters chanted slogans, and Julie De Lima complained to the International Committee of the Red Cross. Luis Jalandoni, chair of the NDF, accused Prime Minister Jan Peter Balkenende of serving the Arroyo and U.S. governments. The National Lawyers Guild denounced the arrest as an attack on dissent and organizing rights. Sison remained in jail until September 13, 2007, when he was released after 17 days of solitary confinement, as the court found insufficient evidence to detain him, specifically that he had "conscious and close cooperation" with those who carried out the killings. On September 27, 2007, Sison appeared before the Hague Court of Appeal on the prosecutor's appeal. On September 28, 2007, Dutch Ambassador Robert Brinks announced that three judicial officials and prosecutor Wim de Bruin would visit the Philippines to review the evidence. The next day, Hong Kong politician Leung Kwok Hung pledged support. On October 3, 2007, the Dutch court dismissed the prosecution's appeal, confirming Sison's freedom, though the police investigation continued and he remained a suspect. The Dutch Public Prosecutor's Office stated that the criminal investigation would continue, separating it from the judicial decision. On May 20, 2008, the Dutch court heard Sison's appeal to extend the investigation until December, after investigators arrived in the Philippines in February and interviewed witnesses; new evidence revealed attempts on his life in 1999 and 2000, and Kintanar's wife, Joy, accused Edwin Garcia of the murder. The court scheduled a verdict on June 10, 2008. On June 5, 2008, the Dutch District Court of The Hague decided in camera that the prosecution could continue its investigation into murders in the Philippines in 2003 and 2004, noting the file still lacked sufficient evidence but that the investigation should continue. In February 2010, the Dutch Public Prosecution Service terminated its investigation and dropped all criminal charges against Sison. Sison met his wife Julie de Lima while both were students at UP Diliman; they married in a civil ceremony in September 1959 and a Catholic ceremony in January 1960 and had four children. Julie de Lima is from the prominent De Lima family of Iriga City, Camarines Sur, and is the aunt of Leila de Lima, who served as Chair of the Commission on Human Rights during Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo's presidency, Secretary of the Department of Justice under Benigno S. Aquino III, and Senator under Rodrigo Duterte. Sison was chair of the International League of Peoples' Struggle and chief political consultant of the NDF. In 2017, President Rodrigo Duterte claimed Sison had colon cancer; Sison, who had been hospitalized at Utrecht University Medical Center in March due to rheumatoid arthritis and Sweet syndrome, stated he had no serious illness. The CPP, NPA, and NDF are considered terrorist organizations by the Philippines' Anti-Terrorism Council. From August 2002, Sison was classified as a "person supporting terrorism" by the United States. The European Court of First Instance ruled in September 2009 to delist him and reverse a decision to freeze his assets. Sison was charged with murder in the Philippines and the Netherlands, but the charges were later dropped. He died in exile in the Netherlands in 2022.

Jose Maria Sison met his wife, Julie de Lima, while both were students at UP Diliman, where they attended the same study groups and grew close, marrying first in a civil wedding in September 1959 and then in a Catholic church wedding in January 1960. The couple had four children. Julie de Lima is from the prominent De Lima family of Iriga City, Camarines Sur, and is the aunt of Leila de Lima, who served as Chair of the Commission on Human Rights during Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo’s presidency, Secretary of the Philippine Department of Justice under Benigno S. Aquino III, and Senator during Rodrigo Duterte’s administration. Sison was the chairperson of the International League of Peoples' Struggle and the Chief Political Consultant of the National Democratic Front of the Philippines (NDFP). In 2017, President Rodrigo Duterte claimed Sison had colon cancer; however, Sison admitted to being hospitalized at Utrecht University Medical Center in March 2017 due to rheumatoid arthritis and Sweet syndrome symptoms and stated he had no serious illness, including cancer. In early 2022, reports surfaced that Sison had died; he immediately refuted the claim. On December 16, 2022, the Communist Party of the Philippines and its news organ Ang Bayan announced Sison’s death after a two-week hospitalization in Utrecht, Netherlands. NDFP executive Luis Jalandoni confirmed Sison died from heart failure after nearly three weeks of hospital treatment, though no further details were provided. Former Senator Jovito Salonga accused Sison of orchestrating the 1971 Plaza Miranda bombing during the Liberal Party convention to compel President Marcos to suspend the writ of habeas corpus and sign Proclamation No. 1081, initiating Martial Law; this accusation originated from former CPP members like Victor Corpuz. The Philippine National Police filed criminal charges against Sison for the bombing, but the case was dismissed for lack of evidence, with the dismissal citing the complainant’s charges were based on speculation. On July 4, 2008, Manila’s RTC Executive Judge Reynaldo Ros took jurisdiction over 1,551-page multiple murder lawsuits against Sison, Satur Ocampo, and Luis Jalandoni after the Supreme Court’s Third Division ordered a change of venue from Hilongos, Leyte RTC Branch 18 for safety reasons. During the alleged incidents, Sison and Ocampo had been under maximum detention by the Marcos regime and were only released in 1986 following the first EDSA uprising. The European Union’s second highest court ruled to delist Sison and the Stichting Al-Aqsa group from the EU terror list because the EU failed to respect their rights when blacklisted. The Luxembourg-based Court of Justice reversed a decision by EU member governments to freeze Sison’s and the Netherlands-based Al-Aqsa Foundation’s assets, citing the EU’s failure to inform them of the reasons for the freeze. Dekker stated that EU lawyers in Brussels could file any appeal. The EU was also ordered to bear all litigation expenses during Sison’s five-year appeal against the Dutch government and the EU. The European Court of Justice’s final judgment removing Sison from the EU terrorist blacklist on September 30, 2009, became final and binding on December 10, 2009, as the EU did not appeal. Court-related documents and legal cases involving Sison in the Philippines are compiled under the Legal Cases section at www.josemariasison.org and can be verified in the archives of the relevant courts. Two biographies have been written about him: one by German writer Dr. Rainer Werning, *The Philippine Revolution: From the Leader's View Point* (1989), and one by Filipina activist Ninotchka Rosca, *At Home in the World* (2004). Two biographical films were produced: *The Guerrilla Is a Poet* (2013), directed by sisters Sari and Kiri Dalena, and *Tibak* (2016), written and directed by journalist Arlyn dela Cruz. After his death, national democratic organizations in Manila launched the Jose Maria Sison School, involving hundreds of youth, union members, and activists in a re-examination of Sison’s teachings. Leftist groups from Berkeley to Rome followed this initiative. Many activists and scholars have continued Sison’s legacy in various ways. On February 15, 2025, key leaders of the national democratic movement launched the Jose Maria Sison Legacy Foundation (TJMSLF) in Utrecht, The Netherlands, to preserve the legacy of the Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP) founder. Maybelle Guerrero has called for revolutionaries to review Sison’s work and to undertake his unfinished tasks, such as reviving the armed city partisan teams to address human rights violators in urban areas.
